A batsman of undoubted class and a captain of tremendous focus, age may be catching up to Michael Clarke as his eventual successor steals the limelight.Dogged by persistent back injuries, Clarke's form with the bat has been scratchy at best, while Steve Smith has caught fire at the crease.Lampooned by former Test paceman Jason Gillespie as having a "glass back", Clarke will look to prove a point in England after a sequence of interrupted series.He made 128 in Adelaide against India in the first Test in December, but then missed the remainder of the four-match series.His three innings in the Caribbean were hardly exemplary as he felt his way back into the Test side.But Clarke's presence and the "Will he? Won't he?" build-up to the World Cup did not derail the Australian side as it claimed a fifth title in March.Clarke played his part in that triumph, scoring a valuable 68 against Sri Lanka in Sydney before making 74 in the successful run-chase against New Zealand in the final.Clarke's inevitable successor as Test captain, Steve Smith has enjoyed Bradman-esque form since his maiden Test century at The Oval in 2013.Since that Ashes Test, Smith has averaged 78.68 with the bat, hitting all nine of his career Test tons so far, including a divine run against India last summer where he scored a century in each Test of the four-match series.He averaged 67.00 at the World Cup - scoring four half-tons as well as a century against India in the semi-final - and his form post-tournament has not let up, with a career high 199 against a poor West Indies side.A dazzling stroke-maker and improviser, Smith can tear apart the world's best bowling attacks, while also possessing the fortitude to hold the fort against spin attacks on treacherous pitches, as he did on his return to the Test side against India in 2013, scoring a patient 92 in Mohali.The unflappable Smith also adds an extra spin option should Australia require it, but his scorching form with the willow has long eclipsed the memory of his leg-spin abilities.David Warner never truly fired on his disrupted tour of England in 2013, and will be looking to make amends on his second Ashes tour.Warner enjoyed only middling form during the recent World Cup with plenty of starts with the bat but failed to capitalise on any, apart from a bullying 178 against associate Afghanistan in Perth.In the summer series against India, Warner began with a bang, notching 145 and 102 in the first Test, but other than a 101 in Sydney, he endured average form.When he fires, Warner is capable of winning whole Test matches single-handedly, but his sporadic form may mean he is seen as a bonus for the team in any given match, with other batsman providing more reliable foundations.Chris Rogers comes into the Ashes series somewhat cold after missing the West Indies tour due to concussion.Rogers provides a rock-solid influence at the top of the order, and has dovetailed well with David Warner in his comparatively short Test career.After a slow start in Adelaide, Rogers proceeded to score a half-ton in each of the remaining six innings of the series in India's tour Down Under.Rogers was picked for the 2013 Ashes tour on the back of his county form and knowledge of local conditions. He will be relishing the chance to open the batting for a side no longer struggling like it did two years ago.All-rounder Shane Watson scored a drought-breaking 176 against England at the Oval in 2013, and looked to be a batsman to be feared once more when he notched 103 against the same team in Perth.But his form with the bat has quietened once again. Mute against the West Indies, he scored just the two half-centuries against India in December.Since having his bowling duties reduced, Watson has also not taken more than two wickets in an innings since a dramatic 5 for 17 against South Africa in 2011.But coach Darren Lehmann insists Watson remains an important gun in Australia's arsenal as a fifth bowling option."You see if a bowler goes down you are left short, so you really need to have that option in your side. We would have liked more runs [from Watson]. I thought he bowled really well [in the West Indies]," Lehmann said.Shaun Marsh had the chance to showcase his credentials as an opening bat on the recent tour of the West Indies, making 112 runs across four innings, including a 69 in Kingston.He will provide competition for Chris Rogers' spot, having batted in the middle order against India in the four-Test series.Against India, Marsh made a number of sizeable scores, run out for 99 at the MCG as well as making 73 in Sydney.But he has yet to reach his potential with the bat in a stop-start international career, and is approaching 1,000 runs after four years of Test cricket.This tour will likely provide his first Test appearance against England, home or away.Adam Voges has been on the periphery of the national side for ages, and he finally made his Test breakthrough with a debut unbeaten 130 against the West Indies in Roseau in June.At 35 years of age, Voges became the oldest man to score a century on debut, and was the first Australian to do it since Shaun Marsh's 141 against Sri Lanka in 2011."People have been saying I'm the oldest guy for a lot of things, so I'll take it," he said.An attacking batsman from Western Australia, he found fame with a maiden one-day century off 62 balls for his state, before making his ODI debut for Australia in 2007 against New Zealand.He would have to wait two years for his next ODI start which saw a run of 13 matches in the national side, before two more hiatuses - one year and two years of length - saw him finally establish himself in 2013 with an unbeaten century against the West Indies at the MCG.The man behind the stumps is likely to be playing in his last Ashes tour and has been a guiding presence in a developing side.He saved Australia's bacon a number of times in the Ashes clean sweepBatting down at seven and eight has seen him endure a lean trot lately, averaging just 15.33 in 19 innings the 2014 tour of South Africa, including three ducks and just one half-century.Some flaws remain in his keeping technique, but he is equally capable of the spectacular behind the stumps, with plenty of edges to come from the likes of Mitchell Starc, Ryan Harris and Mitchell Johnson.An all-rounder of undoubted potential and brother to Test batsman Shaun, Mitchell Marsh faces the biggest moment in his fledgling Test career in an Ashes tour - if he can get into the match XI.A composed 87 in just his second Test against Pakistan in 2014 showcased gave Australian cricket lovers a flash of his watchfulness with the bat, followed by three consecutive innings in the forties against Pakistan and India.Whenever he has caught the eye of selectors, it has been mostly with the bat, and his foray into bowling for Australia has yet to truly mature. Just the one wicket in Tests, and 11 in 17 ODIs for Australia means he will only ever factor as a support role in the immediate future.In a congested middle order, competing with the likes of Michael Clarke, Steve Smith, Shane Watson and his brother Shaun, Mitchell will have a tough time getting into an in-form batting side.The one player yet to debut at full international level for Australia, Peter Nevill may spend the entirety of the Ashes tour in the changing rooms, barring an injury to Brad Haddin.The wicketkeeper has impressed at Sheffield Shield level for New South Wales, making just under 3,000 runs for the Blues since his 2009 debut at an average of 44.27, while taking 163 catches behind the stumps in 54 matches.His time may come with 37-year-old Haddin in the twilight of his career, but that may be well after this series in England.Regardless, Nevill is a solid batsman who has been featured alongside Haddin in New South Wales sides, holding his own as a specialist bat.Pat Cummins is another of Australia's promising flock of young quicks, and if he can stay healthy, he could become a mainstay of the Test team for years to come.Cummins has played just one Test thus far in his career, against South Africa way back in 2011, but it was a highly impressive debut. He ended the match with seven wickets, which included figures of 6 for 79 in the second innings.A series of injuries has curbed his Test career since, but his impressive form upon his return to limited over cricket indicates he is ready to pick up where he left off in the five-day game.Ironically it is Ryan Harris's forced retirement through injury which has opened the door for Cummins' return to the Test arena, via a call-up to the 2015 Ashes squad.Mitchell Starc enjoyed an exceptional World Cup, taking 22 wickets in Australia's title run on home soil.His searing form in the ODI arena is now beginning to seep into Test cricket, where Starc has long struggled to truly convince he belongs.But a regular feed of wickets during the series against India, as well as 10 wickets in two Tests against the West Indies, means Starc is practically demanding to be picked to send down the red ball for his country.A quick left-armer who bowls devastating in-swinging yorkers to right-hand batsmen, Starc should enjoy prodigious movement in the air in English conditions.Former England tweaker Graeme Swann has identified Starc as Australia's dangerman, saying "Mitchell Starc is above and beyond the best match-winning player [Australia have] got at the minute."Forget about the batsmen. If Mitchell Starc bowls well, I don't think England have got any hope of winning the Ashes."For so long compared to Glenn McGrath, the 196cm-tall Josh Hazlewood can no longer shy away from the comparison.Lacking the pace and swing of his seaming counterparts, Hazlewood instead employs his height to extract uncomfortable bounce, and uses his accuracy and movement off the pitch to bamboozle batsmen.It has worked a treat in his embryonic Test career so far, taking five wickets in his debut innings against India in Brisbane, and 24 in his five Tests so far at an average of 19.08.A perfect foil to left-arm team-mates Mitchell Starc and Mitchell Johnson, the right-handed Hazlewood is equally as awkward a customer to deal with as the southpaw contingent of Australia's pace attack.The beginning of 2014 saw Mitchell Johnson resume his bountiful plundering of South Africa with 12 wickets in a single Test at Centurion, but since then, the wickets have dried up somewhat for the moustachioed terror.Johnson took 13 wickets in four Tests against India as his support cast in Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood began to emerge from out of his shadow, and he proceeded to snare just eight in four innings against the West Indies.Nevertheless, Johnson's sheer intimidating presence should be enough to get English batsmen thinking twice, with his nasty repertoire of short and angled deliveries capable of troubling even the most composed batsmen.Johnson still remains invaluable to Australia's lower order as a batsman of genuine talent, having made regular contributions to spark game-winning wags in the team's tail.Former England captain Michael Vaughan has identified off-spinner Nathan Lyon as the chink in Australia's bowling armour, but the country's leading off-spin wicket-taker is taking no notice.Lyon will relish bowling to as many as seven left-handed English batsmen, with many of them looking to keep out his famed - if overly subtle - mystery balls "Jeff" and "Square Jeff"."I'm expecting something pretty similar to last time, probably good batting wickets and hopefully they'll take a bit of spin and hopefully that may play into my hands," Lyon said.Lyon took 12 wickets in the Adelaide Test against India, and his contributions have been consistent throughout recent Test series, taking 42 wickets in total (11 Tests) since the tour of South Africa in early 2014.A talented leg spinner who can procure sharp turn from a short run-up, Fawad Ahmed has a job on his hands if he is to make his Test debut for Australia in the Ashes cauldron.After seeking asylum in 2010 and being used as a regular bowler in the nets for Australia, Ahmed was granted citizenship in 2013 and has since featured in three ODIs and Twenty20s for his adopted country.But the fairytale Test appearance may be on hold for a while longer after coach Darren Lehmann admitted there were enough part-time spinners in the side to negate the need for a second spinner alongside Nathan Lyon.Hope does remain, however, in the eyes of captain Michael Clarke, who believes "Fuzz" will deliver for the national team if given the opportunity.Apart from an appearance against the WICB Presidents' XI, pace schemer Peter Siddle has not featured for Australia since the first Test against India in Adelaide.Years of pushing his body to the limit in heroic displays of stamina have taken their toll on Siddle - long the mortar holding the bricks of Australia's attack together.But 12 wickets spread across five Tests in 2014 hardly saw Siddle breaking down the door to remain in starting contention, as Josh Hazlewood emerged as a pace option and Mitchell Starc came to grips with Test match bowling.Siddle adds depth to the pace department with movement off the seam his featured weapon, while he also has two Test half-tons to his name with the bat.
summary: Ryan Harris is ruled out of the entire Ashes tour after failing to recover from a knee injury and promptly retires from all forms of cricket.

title: Parascale raises $11.37M to help companies control their storage destiny
text:
A startup called Parascale is preparing to launch software that chief executive Sajai Krishanan says will help media companies deal with ever-increasing storage needs. The company has just raised $11.37 in its first round of venture backing.
Computing and storage in the Internet “cloud” are hot right now, with big players like Amazon and Google offering their own cloud services. There are even startups like RightScale (which raised $4.5 million from Benchmark Capital in April) providing software to make managing your Amazon servers easier.
Cupertino, Calif.-based Parascale offers storage management software as well, but it rather than sitting on top of Amazon or another sevice in the cloud, Parascale connects a network of Linux servers that its customers own. As a company grows, and its bandwidth needs increase, owning servers rather than buying space from Amazon or Google allows a company to “control its destiny,” Krishnan says. That’s particularly relevant in light of Amazon’s occasional outages.
Companies like PolyServe (now owned by Hewlett Packard) and Ibrix provide similar services, but Krishnan says those are older companies designed for an earlier wave of computing needs, rather than the intense data demands of online media. For example, he says most competing software is designed to connect a server network with dozens of nodes, while Parascale is designed to connect a network with hundreds of nodes.
The startup is still in testing mode, and according to Krishnan, Parascale’s already-announced customer Blue Coat Systems doesn’t require the massive storage that the company says it will offer. So it’s not certain whether Parascale will really be able to easily manage the hundreds of nodes that Krishnan claims. Still, lead investors Charles River Ventures and Menlo Ventures have found success in the storage market before — with the sales of EqualLogic for $1.4 billion and Spinnaker Networks for $300 million, respectively.
Parascale was seed funded by Amidzad Partners, also an investor in VentureBeat.
The new funding will be spent on the final stages of Parascale’s development, and on marketing once the product has launched, Krishnan says. He predicts that there will be particular demand for the company’s service in four markets that need to store and easily access vast quantities of data — streaming video and audio, movie archiving, oil and gas research and genetic research.

title: 5 Top Tips for Men on Valentines Day
text:
How any man can be a Valentines Hero.
Best case most men are intimidated by Valentines Day. Worst case they resent it. A lot of men feel like Valentines Day is a lose, lose proposition. Expectations for romance are sky high and men as a species are not super comfortable with their ability to deliver. Some men feel high-jacked by a “Hallmark” holiday.
Men feel pressure to spend a lot of money and compete with the romantic displays of other men with their women. No surprise, when the Valentines Day industry encourages this. I saw an ad for flowers yesterday where a woman talked about receiving a floral super gift at work that made all the other ladies jealous. Bottom line many men feel like they are set up to fail. So, what’s a guy to do??? More importantly, what’s a guy to do that doesn’t cost a fortune?
1. Two flowers. A rose first thing in the morning. They’ll cost you four bucks a piece at 7/11. Keep them in your car the night before. Give one to her before you leave the house in the morning and it’ll answer the question, “Did he remember the special day??” Hold the second flower back for later.
2. Yes, the celebration should include a meal. That doesn’t have to mean dinner at the most expensive spot in town. It can be a picnic, indoors or out. It can be a trip down memory lane, like the place you went on your first date. It could be lunch at hotel. Whatever it is, think intimate, vs. expensive.
3. Put pen to paper. Even if you’ve never done it, maybe especially if you’ve never done it, write a love note. Notice, I didn’t say letter, I said note. The recipe is simple, three paragraphs. First, a cherished memory you have of times with her. Second, something you love about her. Third, how she makes you feel. Sign it I love you, and you’re done. Very important note: Give her this note at dinner or deliver it to her office during the day.
4. Jewelery, or chocolate? Maybe none of the neither. Maybe a gift certificate for a massage or pedicure - either by a professional, or better yet, maybe by you. Treat her to something that will leave her feeling pampered and precious. If you opt to buy them, you’re looking at about $50.00. If you opt to offer up the pampering yourself, you better follow through, probably on Valentines evening.
5. Run her a bath. Before bedtime, run her a bath, light some candles in there, and sprinkle the petals from the last rose in the tub. Done.
Follow these five steps and I swear to you - you will be a Valentines Day hero. Which is really what men want - even the ones that hate the holiday.
Lisa Hayes C.Ht. is the Love Whisperer. She is a Law of Attraction Relationship Coach and author of The Passion Plan and Escape from Relationship Hell. She specializes in helping people get the love they want, no matter where they are in their lives. You can find her at her digit home, www.lisamhayes.com. Get her free audio, How to Talk to a Man, HERE.
summary: How any man can be a Valentines Hero.

title: Book review: Debut memoir ‘Burn Down the Ground’ careens from happiness to unimaginable depression, includes run-in with Mark Cuban
text:
Kambri Crews’ debut memoir, Burn Down the Ground, places her firmly in the company of family-dysfunction specialists such as Augusten Burroughs, Jeannette Walls and, especially, Mary Karr, whose 1995 best-seller The Liars’ Club set the bar for tales of dirt-poor Southeast Texas upbringings.
The biting humor of Burn Down the Ground, along with the author’s smooth, natural storytelling, reflect her adult years — she’s been an actress, owns her own PR and production company, and is the comedy booker for 92YTribeca. She knows how to take even the most dire material and wring out of it a rueful chuckle. The child of deaf parents, she notes early in the book, “You know you talk a lot when your deaf family nicknames you ‘Motor Mouth.’”
The book’s title refers to the tradition of burning the brush and deadwood on long-neglected land: You have to destroy the past to give birth to something new. It’s an action, both literal and metaphorical, that her family takes repeatedly.
Young Kambri keeps herself busy with early entrepreneurial projects such as starting her own lending library. “While such a nerdy endeavor might elicit taunts from kids in other neighborhoods, the children on Boars Head greeted my enterprise like I was the ice cream man. They were equally bored and isolated, after all. This was no child’s play; even my parents were frequent patrons. … My mother preferred books like A Separate Peace.”
Peace was something her mother craved, living with Kambri’s frustrated, chronically unemployed and oft-violent father. The book’s narrative toggles between her childhood and her visits to him in a Texas prison, where he’s serving a 20-year-sentence for attempted murder in the stabbing and near-decapitation of his girlfriend after divorcing Crews’ mother.
Crews’ childhood careens from near-normalcy and happiness, as when her parents scrape together a few hundred dollars to buy her a horse, to unimaginable deprivation: When the family’s house trailer is repossessed, the horse has to vacate its tin shack so the family can move in.
“Dad divided the shed in half lengthwise with plasterboard walls. One side was turned into a kitchen with a small living room, where Mom and Dad could sleep on one of our two maroon hide-a-bed sofas. The other side served as a bedroom for [her brother] David and me.”
Toward the end of the book, Crews and her mother move to North Central Texas and into a substantially more stable life. Crews finishes up the book with recollections of her move to New York City. At a comedy show, she meets Dallas billionaire Mark Cuban. He likes her group and takes them on a club tour.
She describes it with typical humor, naiveté-tinged verve — and one heck of a punch line.
“As we walked into one nightclub, Mark sailed past the maitre d’ without checking in. ‘You’re not allowed to do that,’ I said playfully. He patted my hand with a sly grin and whispered in my ear, ‘Kambri, when you live in my world, you can do anything you want.’ I could get used to a world like this.
“That same night, 1,542 miles away, Dad was stabbing Helen.”
Burn Down the Ground
Kambri Crews
(Villard, $25)
summary: A debut author brings wit, insight to her memoir of a dirt-poor Southeast Texas childhood.

title: Fans Like Everything About First Solo Footage, Except Han Solo
text:
Disney and Lucasfilm have released the first trailer for Solo: A Star Wars Story with less than four months to go until the movie hits theaters. The biggest question ahead of seeing this first footage was how Alden Ehrenreich would fare as Han Solo, who was brought to life originally by Harrison Ford and remains one of the most iconic characters in cinema history. This trailer did give us choice bits of the young actor as the famed smuggler and future Rebellion hero and the internet has reacted. Unfortunately, the majority of those reactions are negative.
Casting someone other than Harrison Ford as Han Solo was always an uphill battle, but much of the Star Wars fanbase appear to be hovering over the panic button after seeing this trailer. Even though everything else in this trailer looks fantastic and would appear to be everything we'd want from a Star Wars movie, if Alden Ehrenreich can't sell us on his version of Solo, it could be dead on arrival. Here's what Bleacher Report writer Davie Schilling had to say, expressing concern over some of his line readings in the trailer.
"The element that truly worries me about Solo: A Star Wars Story is Alden Ehrenreich. Some of those line readings in the trailer are *rough*."
Ron Howard took over as director of Solo: A Star Wars Story last year, shortly after Phil Lord and Chris Miller were fired. The duo had filmed nearly all of the movie and it's said that Howard reshot as much as 80 percent of the Star Wars standalone. But it was Lord and Miller who cast Alden Ehrenreich in the role of Han Solo and his casting suited their vision, which ultimately clashed with what Lucasfilm President Kathleen Kennedy wanted. Awards Circuit writer Joseph Braverman feels that Baby Driver star Ansel Elgort, who was one of the hundreds of actors who were considered, would have made for a better fit.
"After watching Baby Driver and then seeing this Solo trailer, I really want to know why they passed up Ansel Elgort for Alden Ehrenreich. Voice and charisma is just not there for me. Sorry."
There were reports that Alden Ehrenreich's acting was a problem and an acting coach was brought on board prior to Ron Howard's reshoots on Solo: A Star Wars Story. Is that why Lucasfilm seems to be hiding his performance as much as possible in the marketing? There was an awful lot of eye candy and set pieces to draw one's attention in this first trailer. But not everyone is concerned. A Twitter user and Star Wars fan who uses the handle @brandonh83 is encouraged by what he's seen.
Related: Solo Honest Trailer Kicks the Star Wars Franchise While It's Down
"Alden Ehrenreich looks FUN as Han. People are too obsessed with him somehow playing a perfect younger FORD. That's not the point. He feels like a younger, looser HAN SOLO. It's about the character. His performance from the trailer makes him seem extremely enjoyable and charming."
Even without the production problems that plagued Solo: A Star Wars Story, doing a young Han Solo movie was always a tough sell. And, as has been pointed out, Alden Ehrenreich is only seven years younger than Harrison Ford was in Star Wars: A New Hope. So he's not really that young. You can check out a bunch of Twitter reactions to Alden Ehrenreich in the Solo: A Star Wars Story trailer for yourself below.

title: They don't all wear capes: 'Amazing Race Canada: Heroes Edition' premiers July 3
text:
Bill Brioux , The Canadian Press
TORONTO -- What makes a hero?
They don't all wear capes and tights or bend steel in their bare hands. On the new season of "The Amazing Race Canada," the kind of 'heroes' viewers will get to know are those who wear military or police uniforms; who work as teachers, nurses, or launch charities.
On "The Amazing Race Canada: Heroes Edition," premiering July 3 on CTV, there are also two retired air force pilots and Toronto Argonauts cheerleaders.
All 10 teams were nominated by friends, family and co-workers. Among those competing are two-time national barrel racing champion Nancy Csabay and three-time Olympian Mellisa Hollingsworth, both from Alberta.
Csabay, who received more than 30 nominations, has wanted to enter the "Amazing Race" for years. "I'm turning 50 this year, so why not?" she says.
Four years ago she was diagnosed with breast cancer. Just don't call her a cancer survivor.
"I don't want to give cancer any more energy than it deserves," she says.
Hollingsworth, 37, won a bronze medal in the women's skeleton at the 2006 Winter Games in Turin, Italy. Her hero is her father, a single dad who she says "tucked me in every night and told me I was his hero."
For Csabay, that was her mom.
"I have so much respect for her," says Csabay, just 17 when her mom died of cancer. "She was a tough, tough lady who endured a lot. I'm so grateful that I'm her daughter."
Soaring into the field are two retired air force pilots from small-town Ontario -- Corey "Chewy" Liddle, 47, and Mark "Happy" LaVerdiere, 48.
LaVerdiere was a Lead Solo pilot for the famed Snowbirds aerobatics team. Liddle was a pilot for the United Nations Humanitarian Air Service. Both served multiple tours in Afghanistan and took part in aid relief there, as well as in Haiti and South Sudan.
As for their nicknames: "Happy" bares a strong resemblance to, as he puts it, "a very handsome actor by the name of Adam Sandler." LaVerdiere says he even golfs like the "Happy Gilmore" star.
An old hockey injury left "Chewy" with a lop-sided gait. That, and, at one time, a headful of shaggy hair and a beard begged comparisons to a certain "Star Wars" Wookie.
Among the younger teams are Argos cheerleaders Leanne Larsen, 25, and Marielle "Mar" Lyon, 26. They've thrown their energy behind cheering for healthy and safe learning environments in schools with the Toronto Argonauts' Huddle-Up anti-bullying program.
Lyon says she was bullied growing up in Thunder Bay, Ont. "The hardest years of my life were from Grade 7 until Grade 10 or 11."
The other teams in this summer's "Heroes" edition of the show:
-Joseph Truong, 23, from Mississauga, Ont., and Akash Sidhu, 22, from Brampton, Ont., are the youngest team. Friends since high school and through their years at York University, they graduated together and created their own non-profit charity business.
-Taylor Callens, 25, and Courtney Callens, 27, are proud to be part of a Canadian family policing legacy. The B.C., brother and sister followed their father into the RCMP - the fourth generation of Callens to do so.
-Courtney Berglind, 28, was a bartender and Adam Kovacs, 29, a firefighter being auctioned off at a fundraiser, when they had their first awkward encounter. The engaged couple from Calgary are both first responders, with Courtney being a nurse.
-Martina Seo, 40, and Phil Seo, 37, are a brother-sister team from North Vancouver. The teacher and banker give to children in need all over the world, volunteering over 10,000 hours in Canada, Kenya, South Africa, Korea, Fiji and the U.S.
-Zainab Ansari, 32, and Monica Demian, 24, are both members of the Royal Canadian Navy. The Greater Toronto Area residents are proud to represent the amazing women who serve in the Canadian Armed Forces.
-Dylan Elias, 28, and Kwame Osei, 34, are out to unite the youth of Fort McMurray, Alta., through athletics and football. The two, who met on rival football fields while studying in Nova Scotia, hope to have a positive impact on inner city kids as well as those struggling on First Nation reserves.
-Childhood cancer survivor Todd Kirk and Anna Holtby, both 24 and engaged, have been friends since high school. Cancer left Todd with noticeable facial differences leading to stares and teasing; neither stopped him from becoming a high school quarterback.
summary: What makes a hero? They don't all wear capes and tights or bend steel in their bare hands. On the new season of "The Amazing Race Canada," the kind of 'heroes' viewers will get to know are those who wear military or police uniforms; who work as teachers, nurses, or launch charities.

title: RBS retreats from face-to-face advice with 550 job cuts
text:
An RBS spokesman said that the retraction from face-to-face advice was partly due to a drop in demand for advice in-person, which had been facilitated by regulatory developments including the retail distribution review (RDR).
In the lead up to the RDR, the bank cut over 600 financial planning roles, around half the service across the country, but created 350 new jobs in the process.
The bank is looking to set up a new direct to consumer platform later this year, however, which it hopes to roll out as an online service to clients with a minimum of £500 to invest.
‘We want to help as many customers as possible invest their money in the right way for them,’ an RBS spokesperson said. ‘The demand for face to face investment advice is changing. Our customers increasingly want to bank with us using digital technology. As a result, we are scaling back our face-to-face advisers and significantly investing in an online investing platform that enables us to help a new group of customers with as little as £500 to invest’.
The cuts to protection advice mean this service will now only be available by phone.
The RBS spokesman said: ‘Due to the gradual decline in the number of customers in our protection business, this service will now be available over the telephone. We will move to this new service on 11 March and will proactively contact all customers to ensure a smooth transition.'
summary: Bank will only offer protection advice over the phone as job cuts while 220 investment advice roles are set to go.

title: Postal service warns of fraud to get your info
text:
(WTNH)- The Postal Inspection Service is warning customers nationwide of fraudulent emails and phone calls.
The fake caller is stating a package that was unable to be delivered. These emails and phone calls are attempting to gather personal identifying information.
The email, which claims to be from the US Postal Service, includes a message related to an attempted or intercepted package delivery. The customer is told to click the link or open an attachment then print the label.
When opened, a malicious virus is installed on the computer. This virus could steal personal identifiers of the customer and compromise the customer’s information.
If a customer receives an email similar to the one described above, they should follow these steps:
-Do not click on the link or open the attachment
-Forward the email to spam@uspis.gov
-Delete the email
Criminals are also contacting potential victims via the phone. When contacted, similar information is provided related to an attempted or intercepted package delivery. The caller attempts to obtain personal identifying information from the customer.
If a customer receives a phone call, they should follow these steps:
Do not provide any personal identifying information to the caller
-Hang up
-Contact your local post office to verify the phone call
-Contact the Postal Inspection Service at 877-876-2455
The Postal Inspection Service is actively investigating these fraudulent emails and phone calls.

title: President Obama to make first visit of his presidency to U.S. mosque
text:
Though in the final year of his presidency, President Barack Obama is continuing to break personal ground by visiting a U.S. mosque for the first time in his presidency.
Obama plans to visit the Islamic Society of Baltimore on Wednesday to meet with leaders of the local Muslim community.
The visit will amount to a public embrace of Muslims by Obama at a time when political discourse against them seems to be growing in some quarters, largely fueled by fears of terrorist acts carried out by extremist groups. The White House said he will go to the Baltimore mosque to "celebrate the contributions Muslim Americans make to our nation and reaffirm the importance of religious freedom to our way of life."
In remarks to be delivered at the mosque, Obama "will reiterate the importance of staying true to our core values: welcoming our fellow Americans, speaking out against bigotry, rejecting indifference and protecting our nation's tradition of religious freedom," the White House said.
overwhelming majority of americans understand of diversity and religious pluralism is one of our greatest strengths https://t.co/AM1JLoA1TI — President Obama (@POTUS) January 14, 2016
so we all need to speak out against bias and stereotypes, to protect the freedom of others, and our own as well. — President Obama (@POTUS) January 14, 2016
Obama has been outspoken in pushing back against calls by Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump and others to block Muslims from being admitted to the U.S. over fears of domestic terrorism linked to radical extremist groups.
Others have cited potential security risks in pushing legislation in Congress to limit the resettlement of refugees from Iraq and Syria, where the Islamic State group is active and from which it has exported its brand of terrorism to other regions of the world.
It was a topic Obama addressed in his final State of the Union address a few weeks ago, saying:
That’s why we need to reject any politics that targets people because of race or religion. This isn’t a matter of political correctness. It’s a matter of understanding what makes us strong. The world respects us not just for our arsenal; it respects us for our diversity and our openness and the way we respect every faith. His Holiness, Pope Francis, told this body from the very spot I stand tonight that “to imitate the hatred and violence of tyrants and murderers is the best way to take their place.” When politicians insult Muslims, when a mosque is vandalized, or a kid bullied, that doesn’t make us safer. That’s not telling it like it is. It’s just wrong. It diminishes us in the eyes of the world. It makes it harder to achieve our goals. And it betrays who we are as a country.
"That’s not telling it like it is."http://on.mash.to/1SNJfE8 Posted by Mashable News on Tuesday, January 12, 2016
Obama has argued that such efforts are wrong and serve only to incite extremist groups, weaken America's leadership around the world and put U.S. security at risk.
"We're not going to build progress with a bunch of phony tough talk, and bluster, and over-the-top claims that just play into ISIL's hands," the president said, using an acronym for the Islamic State. He spoke to House Democrats on Thursday as they strategized at a meeting in Baltimore. "We're not going to strengthen our leadership around the world by allowing politicians to insult Muslims or pit groups of Americans against each other. That's not who we are. That's not keeping America safe."
Obama himself has battled various conservative conspiracy theories that he himself is a Muslim (he is not), a storyline that has reared its head even in this election cycle.
Additional reporting by Mashable.
summary: The visit is part of the president's ongoing efforts to fight back on the anti-Muslim rhetoric that has circulated recently.

title: Letters to the Editor: Aug. 29
text:
End of an era
Regarding the article A comic ending (Aug. 26).
After it opened in 1979, I was a weekly visitor to the Comic Book Collector until the mid-1980s. Eddy Smet and his wife and her parents ran the store. It wasn’t just the place I bought my comics, it was a place to visit. They were interesting folks.
I ended up selling my collection to another London business, City Lights book store. I miss the comics and hardly recognize most of my favourite characters from movies and TV.
Ed Meiller
London
— — —
Political correctness test
As feedback to the request from Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario to rename all John A. Macdonald schools in Ontario, I recommend we request all Ontario school boards halt direct deposits of salary to ETFO staff for the remainder of 2017 and instead, pay them with new Canadian $10 bills featuring — you got it — Macdonald on the front, to be picked up at their local board’s human resources office.
It would be amazing to see how many ETFO members extend their commitment to their facade of political correctness to include not picking up their pay envelope.
Chris Butler
London
— — —
Planning inconsistent
I am curious about the mindset of city hall planners. A developer, who has not yet completed his current project, has been given permission to tear down a perfectly good building on Dundas Street. Meanwhile, a block away, a developer who is ready to build is being denied a demolition permit for an eyesore on King Street.
Consistency? I think not.
Dave Mathers
St. Thomas
— — —
Vote wisely
Eight people have more wealth than the planet’s poorest 3.6 billion human beings. This is the most recent report from Oxfam.
Canadians need to be aware of what can happen to a democracy when a few people control the wealth of a nation. Canadians need to elect political leaders who will work in the interests of the majority of citizens.
Leo Kurtenbach
Saskatoon

title: Whatever comes next for Zimbabwe, don’t expect it to be change
text:
Mnangagwa and his crew were helped in this by factionalism in the MDC, which divided into two main streams after the death of the movement’s founding leader, Morgan Tsvangirai, in February this year.
It was always a triumph of hope over reality to expect that November’s coup against Robert Mugabe would herald a new dawn for democracy in Zimbabwe.
After all, the men who decided it was time for 94-year-old Mugabe to be put out to pasture were the heads of his security establishment that had been running the country behind the scenes for a decade or more.
Their choice to replace Mugabe as President, Emmerson Mnangagwa, has been closely tied to the security junta, called the Joint Operations Command, since Zimbabwean independence in 1980.So any hope that Monday’s election would be free and fair, and that the opposition Movement for Democratic Change (MDC) had a chance of defeating the ruling ZANU-PF was a pipe dream from the start.
There were clashes between outraged MDC supporters and the police and army on Wednesday morning in Harare as early results showed ZANU-PF winning an improbably large majority of the seats in parliament. Reports say at least one person was shot dead as soldiers fired on the crowds, and that tear gas and water cannon were also used to try to disperse the demonstrators.
Results posted by the Electoral Commission gave ZANU-PF 144 seats, the MDC 61, and three seats were yet to be declared.
Results of the vote for the Presidency are unlikely to be published before the weekend. MDC supporters insist their leader, Nelson Chamisa, 40, a lawyer and pastor, beat ZANU-PF’s 75-year-old Mnangagwa.
Delays in publishing results led many opposition supporters to charge that the Electoral Commission was doctoring the outcome.
Foreign election monitors from other African countries and the European Union were allowed into Zimbabwe for the first time in 16 years. They applauded the absence of violence that has marred past elections, but said the campaign was not fought on a level playing field, and that the Electoral Commission was “one sided,” favouring the ruling party.
Mnangagwa and his henchmen allowed foreign observers in because they need some sort of international stamp of approval for the election. Under Mugabe’s nearly 40 years of predatory leadership, Zimbabwe sank from being one of the best organized and most productive countries in Africa to a basket case with worthless currency and most people scrambling to survive in the informal economy
With Mugabe gone, ZANU-PF hopes Zimbabwe can shed its sink-hole image and attract foreign investors to revive the economy.
But it was always Mnangagwa and the ruling party’s intention that the election would be a convincing piece of theatre rather than a true exercise in democracy. State-controlled media and local officialdom were marshalled to the cause of promoting the ZANU-PF campaign and minimising the effectiveness of the MDC efforts.
Mnangagwa and his crew were helped in this by factionalism in the MDC, which divided into two main streams after the death of the movement’s founding leader, Morgan Tsvangirai, in February this year.
That factionalism undoubtedly led to a split in the opposition vote in some, mostly urban constituencies, but it is unlikely to be solely responsible for the large ZANU-PF majority in parliamentary seats.
Zimbabwe has been in reality a country ultimately run by the military – though not a military dictatorship in the purest sense – since its creation in 1980. That was after the white minority regime of what was then Rhodesia, facing defeat in the ten-year civil war, negotiated a settlement for majority rule.
One of the Rhodesian institutions that survived the transfer of power to Mugabe and ZANU-PF was the Joint Operations Command (JOC), set up by Ian Smith and the white regime to manage its campaign in the Bush War.
The JOC members are the Minister of Defence; the Commander of the Zimbabwe Defence Forces; heads of the army, airforce, national police, prison service, the Central Intelligence Organization; and the Governor of the Reserve Bank.
Mnangagwa has been closely associated with the JOC from the beginning. He was Minister of State Security in the years immediately after independence when he oversaw butchering and massacres in Ndebele villages in western Zimbabwe where opposition to ZANU-PF was strong.
At least 10,000 people were killed by the North Korean-trained Fifth Brigade in the three-year campaign called Gukurahundi, “the rain that washes away chaff” in the language of the Shona majority.
Some of the Gukurahundi commanders are now on the JOC.
Mnangagwa was in and out of favour with Mugabe during the 1990s and early 2000s, but he was firmly back in the old president’s good books after 2008 election, when he orchestrated a brutally successful campaign of violence against the MDC.
As a reward, Mnangagwa was made Minister of Defence, which came with the chairmanship of the JOC. He went on to become Vice-President in 2014, but fell out with Mugabe’s ambitious wife, Grace, and her supporters who aimed to corner the presidency when the old man retired or died.
Mnangagwa was fired from the Vice-Presidency on November 6 last year, and wisely fled to South Africa. A week later, on November 15, the Minister of Defence and head of the JOC, Gen. Constantino Chiwenga, ordered Mugabe to be placed under house arrest. ZANU-PF shuffled Mugabe out of office on November 21 and installed Mnangagwa, who had returned from his brief exile once the coup was complete.
Mnangagwa’s nickname is “the crocodile,” from his days as a guerrilla fighter against the Smith regime. There’s nothing in Mnangagwa’s record or personality to suggest he can or will shed his crocodile personality and allow a democratic process that sees him lose power. But it would be delightful to be surprised.

title: Admit it, Canada, you're racist!
text:
Memo from: Prime Minister Justin Trudeau
To: My fellow Canadians
Re: Immigration
It has come to my attention that despite my best efforts to divert you from my disastrous economic record by playing the “Islamophobia” card, too many of you still aren’t getting the message.
Why, just the other day I read the results of a Forum Research poll that said 44% of you believe that we should not allow asylum seekers who enter Canada illegally to seek asylum in Canada.
That compares to only 36% of you who believe we should allow asylum seekers who enter Canada illegally to seek asylum in Canada, and 20% of you who are undecided.
To be blunt about it, what the hell is wrong with 44% of you?
Were your grandfathers all Nazis or something?
How can I possibly continue to make Canadian businesses uncompetitive by imposing a national carbon price on them when our largest trading partner, the United States, doesn’t have one, if 44% of you don’t understand how vital it is to the future of Canada that we allow asylum seekers who are entering the country illegally to seek asylum in Canada?
Here I and my Liberal government have been working hard on your behalf tripling the deficit I told you I would bring in before the 2015 election, while calling out the Conservatives for not unanimously supporting an anti-Islamophobia motion they unanimously supported four months ago, and this is the thanks I get?
I must say that speaking as a feminist, who, as my Sophie says, is one of “the boys and men in our lives who encourage us to be who we truly are, who treat girls and women with respect, and who aren’t afraid to speak up in front of others”, I am deeply disappointed in you.
And while we’re at it, what the hell was with that Forum poll last September that showed two-thirds of you support Conservative leadership contender Kellie Leitch’s call for screening prospective immigrants for anti-Canadian values?
I have to tell you, it’s things like this that make me wonder whether all my efforts on your behalf meeting with Chinese billionaires at Liberal fundraising events to champion the middle-class, and vacationing at the Aga Khan’s private island in the Bahamas over the Christmas-New Year’s break, are worth it.
How dare two-thirds of you agree with Kellie Leitch!
Haven’t you people read the columns of practically ever newspaper pundit in Canada about how racist that is, like about 15,000 times, especially during slow news weeks?
If I didn’t know any better, I would say you people don’t trust the media anymore.
How many times do I have to tell you that a Canadian is a terrorist is a Canadian before it sinks in?
Are you not aware of the great Conservative thinker William F. Buckley’s observation that liberals, “claim to want to give a hearing to other views, but then are shocked and offended to discover that there are other views”, which I and my party wholeheartedly agree with, by the way?
Indeed, I’m thinking of making it our campaign slogan for the 2019 federal election.
So, to sum up, I just want you to know, my fellow Canadians, how deeply disappointed I am in you.
Next thing you know, you’ll be burning crosses on the lawns in Prince George.

title: New band of the day – No 1,074: Alphabet Saints
text:
Pop and rock New band of the week Alphabet Saints (No 1,074) Think of journalists who've gone on to form pop bands, and you'll realise there's form here ... To the letter ... Alphabet Saints. Photograph: Nick Clark/GG Gallery
Hometown: London.
The lineup: Robert Christie (vocals, guitar), Hamilton Lee (instruments).
The background: Writing about rock'n'roll is the new rock'n'roll: discuss. We all know about the transition Neil Tennant, Chrissie Hynde and Morrissey made from penning missives for the pop press to actual pop stardom, but more recently there has been a spate of young acts – Emmy the Great, Tyler, the Creator, Ben Howard, Leopard of Honour, Jamie Woon – who either studied journalism or, as in Tyler's case, intended to publish their own magazine before making the move to musician. We know it's traditional to dismiss journalists as frustrated rockers, but it works both ways: we got collared at a gig a few months back by Elizabeth Sankey of Summer Camp, who declared her wish to fulfill her lifelong ambition and work for a certain newspaper beginning with "G". Clue: it wasn't the Grantham Journal. And why not? It's one of those jobs that reminds you of that old adage, "Find something you love to do and you'll never work again." Although if we ever have to interview the Black Crowes, we may be forced to reconsider.
Robert Christie is both journalist and musician, and you might be able to tell because there are torrents of words all over Raptureland, his debut album with Alphabet Saints, the duo he formed last year with ex-Transglobal Underground multi-instrumentalist Hamilton Lee. And they're virtually all audible. Christie's teasing croon – his voice suggesting the odd cigarette has been smoked, allowing us to use the phrase "nicotine-ravaged" for the first time in ages – invites us to pay attention as the lyrics present a tumble of images. Often, he does this not rapping but speed-talking thing, not just for a bit, a la Iggy's "Jesus, this is Iggy" or Oakey's "So this is Phil talking", but for extended sections of the songs. It reminds us of the title track to Paddy McAloon's sadly neglected but wonderful 2003 solo album, I Trawl the Megahertz, where a voice – female – recited verse over beautiful music. Here, Christie, flanked by girls (cooing sidewomen Lucy Castro and George Pringle), plays the lead poet-cum-noir private dick raking over the detritus of failed affairs, searching for clues, narrating like it's going out of fashion, which it did circa the Doors' American Prayer. You make an effort – actually strain – to hear what he's saying. He might be talking about "interrogation techniques" or "gravitational forces". Other times, it might be Stockholm Syndrome or the loss of faith. At one point, he rhymes inconsequential and existential. At another, he declares, "Let the garden grow", and somewhere Voltaire is smiling. Always, there is a concerted attempt to give pretentiousness a good name.
And it's all set to a soundtrack that's like synthed-up glam – think Eno-ised electronica rather than ChinniChap meets the Chemicals – or trip-hop torch songs, like Tindersticks in a tussle with Barry Adamson. It has been described as "foot-stomping motorik art-pop", which is another handy thing about rock writers becoming musicians, and vice versa: they get to save money on the press releases. It's obsessively observant of a particular era, of Bowie and Eno, Reed and Cale; there's even a song called European Girl. Well, of course there is. It's fastidiously futuristic in a 1972 way, looking back to a time when they looked forward to a now that wasn't overly focused on then. But it's filtered through an electronic present that, although it doesn't exactly acknowledge contemporary developments in dubstep and the latest stage in the hardcore continuum, does take in droning atmospherica (the Map) and drum'n'garage (Fling). Helpless Victim makes us think of Tyler, the Creator if he was a fortysomething lounge lizard from Rhyl. What's in the Cat (Is in the Kitchen) is techno-fied Roxy/Sparks. Bowie and Eno loom large over the title track, as they do everywhere. "Right now," sings Christie, "I don't look down." The vertigo of infatuation, the chaos of desire. Don't be fooled by the talk of exit strategies – he's singing about love. And it's making him do strange things. "I put my face/ Right through the sugar glass," he tells us on Carry on Marianne. He must be out of his brilliant mind.
The buzz: "Channels the spirit of early Suicide, Eno-era Roxy, Lou Reed and Bowie circa Station to Station" – independent.co.uk.
The truth: Múm might have gone to Iceland, but this rock-writing daddio's gone to Raptureland.
Most likely to: Make you go "Aaaah!"
Least likely to: Make you go "Zzzzzz ..."
What to buy: Raptureland is out now on Go Gentle.
File next to: Bowie, Roxy, Blue Nile, Paddy McAloon.
Links: soundcloud.com/alphabet-saints.
Tuesday's new band: Ayshay.

title: Burbank school board reaffirms district as 'safe' for all students, regardless of immigration status
text:
Several local parents broke out in applause during a Burbank school board meeting last week after board members passed a resolution that reaffirms a safe and equitable environment for all students, regardless of their immigration status.
Titled "Reaffirming a Safe and Nondiscriminatory School Environment," the resolution was brought to the school board for consideration last Thursday following California state officials' desire for school districts to be declared "safe havens" for students and their families.
The board passed the resolution with a 5-0 vote.
Join the conversation on Facebook >>
State officials began pressing school districts to pass resolutions in December, before President Donald Trump issued a ban last month on the entry of refugees and citizens from seven Muslim-majority countries into the United States. The ban has since been blocked and met with skepticism from federal appeals court judges.
Burbank school officials said they sought to make it clear to residents that district employees "shall not inquire about a student's immigration status" and that "district personnel shall treat all students equitably," according to the resolution.
"I don't want there to be confusion in our schools. Our responsibility is to have safe learning environments. I find that this resolution clarifies that," said Burbank Unified Supt. Matt Hill. "There are families that have come to me privately saying, 'I am concerned.' If we have not walked in their shoes, then we do not know what they're going through."
Hill said some residents criticized the resolution for being "redundant," but Burbank parent Chris Cookson supported the resolution.
"We have a diverse and strong school district," she told the school board. "It is important that we put the well-being of our children — all of our children — first. Last spring, my 8-year-old son came to me scared. He was legitimately frightened that a friend of his would be deported if Trump was elected because she's Mexican. Even the little ones pick up on the political climate right now in our country. But this should not affect them."

title: BMC considers connecting Carter Road promenade to Joggers’ Park in Mumbai
text:
Soon, people in Bandra may have a longer stretch to walk and jog on. The Mumbai civic body is considering connecting Carter Road promenade and Joggers’ Park, which are adjacent to each other, through a pedestrian path. This would increase the length of the track to 2.2km from the present 1.6km.
The idea has been mooted by Yuva Sena leader Aaditya Thackeray. If the plan works out, a 550-metre-long path will connect the two popular spots.
In a tweet on Friday, Thackeray said he has submitted the plan to Mumbai mayor Vishwanath Mahadeshwar and municipal commissioner Ajoy Mehta. “The park is separated from the promenade by a mere 10 minutes. If combined, the peripheral length for walkers, joggers, and tourists will be 2.2km,” his proposal said.
Have submitted a plan to the Mayor & Municipal Commissioner to create a pedestrian connector betn Jogger’s Park and Carter Road (divided by roughly 10m) that will extend the jogging way from 1.6 km to 2.2 km. Just a small intervention planned by my friend Alan.@AJARCHITECTSS pic.twitter.com/OByxQCt8yQ — Aaditya Thackeray (@AUThackeray) December 7, 2017
The scenic Carter Road promenade is maintained by Bandra Residents Association. The plan to extend the promenade was originally proposed by AJ Architects, a city-based landscape design firm.
First Published: Dec 08, 2017 12:28 IST
summary: Yuva Sena leader Aaditya Thackeray has mooted the idea to link the two spots in Bandra frequented by walkers and joggers

title: Zimbabwe: I'll Boot Out Chinese
text:
MDC-T president Nelson Chamisa yesterday said if voted into power he will expel Chinese investors and cancel deals Government signed with the world's second largest economy running into billions of dollars.
Mr Chamisa made the remarks at Dzivarasekwa Stadium during the Zimbabwe Congress of Trade Unions organised Workers Day celebrations.
The celebrations largely turned out to be an MDC-T rally.
Zimbabwe and China have signed several deals running into billions of dollars spanning from energy, roads and general infrastructure development.
"I have seen the deals that Ngwena (President Mnangagwa's (nickname) has entered into with China and others, they are busy asset-stripping the resources of the country.
"I have said beginning September when I assume office I will call the Chinese and tell them the deals they signed are unacceptable and they should return to their country," Mr Chamisa said.
He said his party wanted genuine investment that benefited the people.
The Chinese have assisted the country in various projects that include the extension of the Kariba South Hydro Power Station which added 300MW to the national grid, the ongoing rehabilitation of the Morton Jaffray Water Works that supply water to Harare and dormitory towns of Chitungwiza and Norton.
They have also provided funding for the extension of Victoria Falls International Airport that has seen tourist arrivals increase while funds have also been secured for the expansion of Robert Gabriel Mugabe International Airport and Hwange Thermal Power Station and construction of a new parliament building .
Mr Chamisa reiterated his promise to introduce bullet trains and construct 'spaghetti' roads and adopt e-government that would make it easy to access birth certificates and other records.
"I am talking of spaghetti roads, but some do not understand it, I am talking of bullet trains, some do not understand it. Yes, vision is not for all, but provision is for all.
"Support me in my vision and you will get your provision," said Mr Chamisa.
Meanwhile, Mr Chamisa admitted that they were abusing the courts in their battle for use of party name and symbols with the Dr Thokozani Khupe led faction.
Mr Chamisa and his MDC-T faction had their urgent chamber application seeking the High Court to bar Dr Khupe from using the party name and its symbols dismissed.
Justice Francis Bere ruled that the matter was not urgent adding it was best dealt with through arbitration.
"There is this story of our female former friend from Bulawayo whom some think may mess our things, but don't be afraid, we have finished with that issue and it will not cause confusion," he said.
"We are going to sit down with her to prepare our symbols so that there won't be any confusion when people go to vote, so don't be afraid when you see us approaching the courts it's a trick we are playing. It's skill of the game so don't be afraid that we don't have a plan we are ahead on that one."
After Justice Bere's ruling, Mr Chamisa attacked the judgment saying it was political, but has since appealed to the Supreme Court.
The MDC-T split following the death of founding leader Morgan Tsvangirai with Dr Khupe saying she was the legitimate heir as the only elected deputy of the former prime minister while Mr Chamisa says he was chosen by the party's National Council to be president until their congress scheduled for next year.
summary: MDC-T president Nelson Chamisa yesterday said if voted into power he will expel Chinese investors and cancel deals Government signed with the world's second largest economy running into billions of dollars.

title: Russian spy Chapman launches weekly TV show
text:
MOSCOW, Jan 21 (Reuters Life!) - Russian spy Anna Chapman launched her own weekly TV show on Friday, in her latest public foray since she was deported by the United States last July in a Cold War-style swap.
The 28-year-old redhead has posed in lingerie, attended a space launch and even had a sing-a-long with Prime Minister Vladimir Putin since she returned to Russia following her arrest and expulsion with nine other Russian sleeper agents.
“I will reveal all secrets,” Chapman said on the one-hour, nightly show “Mysteries of the World with Anna Chapman,” which aired on the private Russian channel REN TV.
Dressed in a black and red velvet dress, Chapman reported on a “miracle” baby from Russia’s Dagestan region in the mainly Muslim North Caucasus, where an Islamist insurgency is raging.
In 2009 media reports about the baby had caused a frenzy in the region when imams said pinkish scrawled verses from the Koran had appeared and faded on the child’s body every few day. Regional experts dismissed the claims, saying the impoverished, violence-torn region was clinging to any hint of hope.
Chapman became one of Russia’s most famous spies when photographs she posted on social networking site Facebook were plastered across the front pages of tabloid newspapers around the world.
Although celebrated by the Kremlin and Russian media, the Russian spy ring was reported to have failed to secure any major intelligence before their arrests. (Reporting by Amie Ferris-Rotman and Ludmila Danilova; Editing by Patricia)

title: Supreme Court to hear Anna Nicole Smith estate case
text:
Anna Nicole Smith arrives with her lawyer Howard Stern for her hearing at the Supreme Court in Washington February 28, 2006. REUTERS/Chris Kleponis

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The Supreme Court said on Tuesday that it would decide whether Anna Nicole Smith’s estate should get part of the fortune that the former Playboy model, who died in 2007, sought from her late Texas oil baron husband. It marked the second time the nation’s highest court has agreed to consider the long-running legal battle involving the former topless dancer and Texas billionaire J. Howard Marshall, whom Smith married in 1994 when she was 26 and he was 89. The Supreme Court in 2006 gave Smith another chance to try to collect the millions of dollars she said that her late husband had promised her before his death after 14 months of marriage. But a U.S. appeals court in California ruled in March that Smith’s estate could get none of the $300 million that she had sought. It was a victory for the estate of Pierce Marshall, the son of the Texas oil tycoon who was worth an estimated $1.6 billion. Pierce Marshall died in 2006. Smith died of a drug overdose in 2007 and was survived by her infant daughter. Smith’s onetime lawyer and boyfriend, Howard K. Stern, is serving as executor of her estate. Smith’s 4-year-old daughter, Dannielynn Birkhead, would stand to benefit if the court rules for Smith’s estate. Dannielynn is being raised by Larry Birkhead, who sued to prove his paternity after Stern was originally listed as the father on her birth certificate. Stern and two of Smith’s doctors are currently on trial in Los Angeles, accused of giving her prescription drugs before her death. All three defendants have pleaded not guilty. Both the prosecution and the defense have rested their cases and the judge is considering whether to dismiss some of the charges. Marshall’s will left nearly all his money to his son and nothing to Smith. Smith challenged the will and claimed that her husband had promised her more than $300 million. The Supreme Court is expected to hear arguments in the case early next year, with a decision likely by June. The earlier Supreme Court ruling only addressed whether federal courts can decide the Smith’s claims, not the merits of her arguments that she should get the money. The issue for the Supreme Court in the latest appeal involved whether the appeals court in its ruling improperly limited the power of federal bankruptcy judges in considering such claims.
summary: The Supreme Court said on Tuesday that it would decide whether Anna Nicole Smith's estate should get part of the fortune that the former Playboy model, who died in 2007, sought from her late Texas oil baron husband.

title: Playlist: 10 tracks you need to hear
text:
Listen to ten of our favourite new tracks below, including songs by Daft Punk, Empire Of The Sun, Foxes and Cassie.
Daft Punk: 'Get Lucky' (release date tbc)
Hype can be a dangerous thing, but in the instance of Daft Punk's upcoming album, new song 'Get Lucky' more than delivers. Pharrell offers his ice-cool vocals to this effortlessly smooth funk number, which marks a very welcome return for the French electronic duo. LC
Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
Cassie: 'Rockabyebaby' mixtape (out now)
Quite why Cassie's long-awaited mixtape - which features the likes of Rick Ross, Wiz Khalifa, Fabolous and Ester Dean - hasn't been released as a proper album is anyone's guess, but if it's anything to go by, the ever-delayed LP will be an absolute corker. Listen to the collection in full below. RC
It's been five years since Empire Of The Sun's last record, but they haven't lost their penchant for a swirling synth number. Their new track contains as much fantastical and euphoric electronica as their debut, and then some.
Coastal Cities: 'Entropic' (out June 3)
Buckinghamshire quintet Coastal Cities have been catching the ears of critics with their '80s revival funk spin on traditional indie rock. The effect of such blending on their latest track 'Entropic' makes it fitting for any moment this summer; from road trips and festivals to sticky club dancefloors. RC
Sebastian Ingrosso ft.Tommy Trash, John Martin: 'Reload' (out June 30)
As the sun finally starts to show its face on UK shores, so do the world's top DJs put forward their bid for this summer's anthem. Swedish producer Sebastian Ingrosso's newest effort ticks all the necessary boxes: emotive lyrics, soaring verses and a drop that insists you lose it on the dancefloor. RC
Foxes: 'Beauty Queen' (release date tbc)
When she's not appearing on Zedd or Fall Out Boy's latest albums, Foxes is creating her own brand of sky-soaring pop. She delivers another rousing anthem with ethereal number 'Beauty Queen', reinforcing her as one of music's most promising new stars.
MONSTA: 'Messiah' (out May 6)
Despite their band name, there is nothing scary about MONSTA's soul-drenched vibes. Flanked by piano and heavy beats, the soul-meets-bass act follows in the footsteps of Rudimental in mashing together the genres for maximum effect. LC
TNGHT: 'Acrylics' (out now)
EDM duo TNGHT are poised to blow up in the US this year, with Kanye West, Lil Wayne and Kendrick Lamar all laying claim to their trippy-yet-highly-addictive beats. Their latest track 'Acrylics' has a touch of the '90s hardcore about it, but its cinematic production feels strictly 2013. RC
Fantasia ft. Kelly Rowland, Missy Elliott: 'Without Me' (US release date: April 23)
Former American Idol winner Fantasia Barrino has never attempted to crack the UK market, but if the latest jam from her forthcoming LP Side Effects Of You - which features Kelly Rowland and Missy Elliott - is anything to go by, we suggest she strikes while the iron is scorching. RC
Story Books: 'Simple Kids' (released April 29)
Fresh from performing at SXSW, Story Books are preparing to release their debut EP later this month. The band have gained support from Zane Lowe for their brand of restrained rock, which mixes hollered piano lines with swirling guitar riffs. LC
